steps.text: We start with a very simple initial value problem:
steps.explanation:
The solution decays very fast: at \(t = 0.1\) it is already \(e^{-5} \approx 0.007\), and after that practically zero. Completely harmless behaviour.

Now we compute with the explicit Euler method and the sensible-looking step size \(h = 0.05\). Each step multiplies by \(1 + h \cdot (-50) = 1 - 2.5 = -1.5\):
\(1,\ -1.5,\ 2.25,\ -3.375,\ 5.06,\ -7.59, \ldots\)

The approximation oscillates with growing amplitude – it explodes, although the true solution tends to zero!
steps.section: Chapter 1 · A harmless problem that explodes
steps.insight: Explicit methods can explode for decaying solutions if the step size is too large.

steps.text: With a smaller step size it works: at \(h = 0.01\) the factor is \(1 - 0.5 = 0.5\), and the values \(1, 0.5, 0.25, \ldots\) decay nicely.
steps.explanation:
Where is the limit? And why is this a real problem – couldn't one simply choose a small \(h\)?

The problem shows up in systems with fast and slow components. Example: in a chemical reaction an intermediate product decays within milliseconds, while the final product forms over hours. After the first milliseconds the fast component has long gone – the solution is smooth and changes only slowly. Yet it forces an explicit method to take millisecond steps for the entire hours.

Such problems are called stiff. They occur all the time: chemistry, electronics (circuits), heat conduction, mechanics with very stiff springs.

Our roadmap:
1. Test equation and stability function
2. Stability regions in the complex plane
3. Implicit methods: implicit Euler and the trapezoidal rule
4. What exactly is stiffness?
5. Multistep methods: Adams and BDF
steps.section: Chapter 1 · A harmless problem that explodes
steps.insight: Stiff problems: rapidly decaying components force explicit methods to take tiny steps – even when the solution has long become smooth.

steps.text: To study stability one uses a simple test equation:
steps.explanation:
The exact solution \(y(t) = e^{\lambda t}\,y(0)\) decays, since \(|e^{\lambda t}| = e^{\text{Re}(\lambda)\,t} \to 0\).

Why this equation? A linear system \(y' = Ay\) decouples (using the eigenvectors of \(A\)) into exactly such equations – one for each eigenvalue \(\lambda\) of \(A\). And nonlinear systems behave locally like their linearisation. So whoever understands the test equation understands the essentials.

Complex \(\lambda\) are needed for oscillations: \(\lambda = -a \pm i\omega\) describes a damped oscillation.
steps.section: Chapter 2 · Test equation and stability function
steps.insight: Test equation \(y' = \lambda y\): each eigenvalue of a system behaves like this equation.

steps.text: Applying a one-step method to the test equation turns each step into a multiplication by a number \(R(z)\) that depends only on \(z = h\lambda\):
steps.explanation:
\(R\) is called the stability function of the method.

Explicit Euler: \(y_{k+1} = y_k + h\lambda y_k = (1 + h\lambda)\,y_k\), so
\(R(z) = 1 + z\)

After \(k\) steps: \(y_k = R(z)^k\,y_0\). The approximation decays exactly when
\(|R(z)| < 1\)

This is the stability condition. For \(\lambda = -50\) and \(h = 0.05\): \(z = -2.5\), \(|R| = |1 - 2.5| = 1.5 > 1\) – unstable. For \(h = 0.01\): \(z = -0.5\), \(|R| = 0.5 < 1\) – stable.
steps.section: Chapter 2 · Test equation and stability function
steps.insight: Stability function \(R(z)\), \(z = h\lambda\): the method is stable if \(|R(z)| \le 1\).

steps.text: For real negative \(\lambda\), explicit Euler gives a simple step-size condition:
steps.explanation:
For \(\lambda = -50\): \(h \le \frac{2}{50} = 0.04\).

\(\begin{array}{c|c|c} h & R = 1 - 50h & \text{behaviour} \\ \hline 0.01 & 0.5 & \text{decays monotonically} \\ 0.03 & -0.5 & \text{decays, alternating sign} \\ 0.04 & -1 & \text{jumps } \pm 1 \text{, does not decay} \\ 0.05 & -1.5 & \text{explodes} \end{array}\)

Important: this limit has nothing to do with accuracy! It holds even when the solution is already practically zero and one could actually take large steps.
steps.section: Chapter 2 · Test equation and stability function
steps.insight: Explicit Euler for real \(\lambda < 0\): stable only for \(h \le \frac{2}{|\lambda|}\).

steps.text: And the better explicit methods from the last lesson?
steps.explanation:
As with \(y' = y\) in the last lesson, these are the beginnings of the Taylor series of \(e^{z}\) – naturally, since the exact solution multiplies by \(e^{h\lambda}\) per step.

On the negative real axis they are stable for
• Heun: \(-2 \le z \le 0\) – just as narrow as Euler!
• RK4: \(-2.79 \le z \le 0\) – only slightly better.

The fundamental problem: for all explicit Runge–Kutta methods \(R(z)\) is a polynomial. And every polynomial becomes arbitrarily large for large \(|z|\). No explicit method is stable for arbitrarily large step sizes.
steps.section: Chapter 2 · Test equation and stability function
steps.insight: All explicit methods have a bounded stability region. Higher order hardly helps.

steps.text: Quick check: a system has the eigenvalue \(\lambda = -1000\). What is the largest step size explicit Euler may use? And RK4?
steps.explanation:
• Euler: \(h \le \frac{2}{1000} = 0.002\)
• RK4: \(h \le \frac{2.79}{1000} \approx 0.0028\)

To compute up to \(t = 10\), Euler needs at least \(5000\) steps, RK4 about \(3600\) steps with 4 evaluations each, i.e. about \(14\,000\) evaluations.

Yet \(e^{-1000t}\) has already dropped to \(e^{-10} \approx 5 \cdot 10^{-5}\) at \(t = 0.01\). 99.9 % of the computing work goes into stability alone, not into accuracy.
steps.section: Chapter 2 · Test equation and stability function
steps.insight: For large \(|\lambda|\), stability determines the step size – not accuracy.

steps.text: For complex \(\lambda\) one draws the set of all stable \(z\) in the complex plane – the stability region:
steps.explanation:
Explicit Euler: \(|1 + z| \le 1\) is a disc with centre \(-1\) and radius \(1\).

The animation shows how \(z = h \cdot (-50)\) moves to the left on the real axis as \(h\) grows: at \(h = 0.01\), \(z = -0.5\) (inside, stable), at \(h = 0.05\), \(z = -2.5\) (outside, unstable).

The method is stable for a given problem if \(h\lambda\) lies in the stability region for all eigenvalues \(\lambda\). You can picture it like this: the eigenvalues are scaled by \(h\) and have to fit into the region.
steps.insight: Stability region: all \(z = h\lambda\) with \(|R(z)| \le 1\). All scaled eigenvalues must fit inside.

steps.text: This also explains an observation from the last lesson: for the spring oscillator \(y'' = -y\) the amplitude kept growing with explicit Euler.
steps.explanation:
The system \(y' = v\), \(v' = -y\) has the eigenvalues \(\lambda = \pm i\) – purely imaginary (undamped oscillation).

So \(z = h\lambda = \pm ih\) lies on the imaginary axis. There:
\(|R(z)| = |1 \pm ih| = \sqrt{1 + h^2} > 1\)

The imaginary axis lies (except at the point \(0\)) entirely outside the Euler disc. For any step size, however small, the amplitude grows by the factor \(\sqrt{1 + h^2}\) per step – exactly what we computed there.

Oscillation problems therefore need methods whose stability region contains a piece of the imaginary axis (for example RK4: about \(|z| \le 2.8\) on the imaginary axis).
steps.insight: Oscillations have imaginary eigenvalues. Explicit Euler is never stable there.

steps.text: Quick check: a system has the eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 = -1\) and \(\lambda_2 = -10 + 10i\). Is explicit Euler with \(h = 0.1\) stable?
steps.explanation:
Check \(|1 + h\lambda| \le 1\) for both:
• \(\lambda_1\): \(|1 - 0.1| = 0.9 \le 1\) ✓
• \(\lambda_2\): \(|1 + 0.1 \cdot (-10 + 10i)| = |1 - 1 + i| = |i| = 1 \le 1\) – exactly on the boundary.

So with \(h = 0.1\) the method is just barely (borderline) stable. The second component does not decay, although it should. With \(h = 0.09\): \(|1 - 0.9 + 0.9i| = \sqrt{0.01 + 0.81} \approx 0.906\) ✓ – safely stable.
steps.insight: Checking stability: test \(|R(h\lambda)| \le 1\) for every eigenvalue.

steps.text: The way out: implicit methods. The implicit Euler method takes the slope at the end of the step instead of at the start:
steps.explanation:
The difference from explicit Euler is small but decisive: \(y_{k+1}\) appears on both sides of the equation. It cannot simply be computed; an equation must be solved in each step – hence “implicit”.

Geometrically: you look for the point at the end of the step whose tangent leads back exactly to the current point.
steps.insight: Implicit Euler: \(y_{k+1} = y_k + h\,f(t_{k+1}, y_{k+1})\) – \(y_{k+1}\) appears on both sides.

steps.text: For the test equation the equation can be solved directly:
steps.formula: y_{k+1} = y_k + h\lambda\,y_{k+1} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad (1 - h\lambda)\,y_{k+1} = y_k \quad \Longrightarrow \quad R(z) = \frac{1}{1 - z}
steps.explanation:
For \(\text{Re}\,z < 0\), \(|1 - z| > 1\), so \(|R(z)| < 1\). The implicit Euler method is stable on the entire left half-plane – for every step size!

Example \(y' = -50y\), \(h = 0.05\): \(R = \frac{1}{1 + 2.5} \approx 0.2857\).
Values: \(1,\ 0.286,\ 0.082,\ 0.023,\ 0.0067, \ldots\) – decaying smoothly like the exact solution.

Even with \(h = 1\): \(R = \frac{1}{51}\), the solution is practically zero after one step – correct!

A method whose stability region contains the whole left half-plane is called A-stable.
steps.insight: Implicit Euler: \(R(z) = \frac{1}{1 - z}\), stable for all \(\text{Re}\,z \le 0\) – A-stable.

steps.text: The price of stability: an equation has to be solved in every step. For a linear system \(y' = Ay\) it is a linear system of equations:
steps.explanation:
With a fixed step size the matrix \(I - hA\) is always the same. Its LU decomposition is computed once (\(O(n^3)\)), and each step only requires solving two triangular systems (\(O(n^2)\)) – see “Gaussian Elimination & LU Decomposition”.

An explicit step, by contrast, costs only one matrix–vector multiplication. So implicit steps are more expensive – but much larger steps can be taken.
steps.insight: Implicit for linear systems: solve \((I - hA)y_{k+1} = y_k\) per step, with an LU decomposition computed once.

steps.text: For nonlinear equations Newton's method is needed in each step. Example: \(y' = -y^3\), \(y(0) = 1\), one step with \(h = 0.5\):
steps.explanation:
Newton with \(g'(y) = 1 + 1.5y^2\) and starting value \(y_0 = 1\) (the old value is a good starting value):
• \(1 - \frac{0.5}{2.5} = 0.8\)
• \(0.8 - \frac{g(0.8)}{g'(0.8)} \approx 0.77143\)
• \(\approx 0.770917\)

So \(y_1 \approx 0.7709\). Exactly, \(y(0.5) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.7071\) – the large step size costs accuracy (order 1), but the result is reasonable. Explicit Euler would have given \(1 - 0.5 = 0.5\).

In practice 1 to 3 Newton steps per time step usually suffice.
steps.insight: Implicit methods for nonlinear ODEs: solve a nonlinear equation with Newton in every time step.

steps.text: Quick check: perform one implicit Euler step for \(y' = -10y\), \(y(0) = 1\) with \(h = 0.5\). Compare with explicit Euler.
steps.explanation:
Implicit: \(y_1 = \frac{y_0}{1 - h\lambda} = \frac{1}{1 + 5} \approx 0.167\).
Explicit: \(y_1 = (1 + h\lambda)\,y_0 = (1 - 5) \cdot 1 = -4\).

Exact: \(e^{-5} \approx 0.0067\).

The implicit result is not very accurate (the step size is large), but it behaves correctly: positive and smaller than before. The explicit result is completely wrong – negative and larger than the initial value.
steps.insight: Implicit: qualitatively correct even with large steps. Explicit: completely wrong with too large steps.

steps.text: The implicit Euler method has only order 1. An A-stable method of order 2 is the implicit trapezoidal rule:
steps.formula: y_{k+1} = y_k + \frac{h}{2}\Big( f(t_k, y_k) + f(t_{k+1}, y_{k+1}) \Big)
steps.explanation:
As in Heun's method, the average of the slopes at the start and at the end is taken – but the slope at the end is not estimated, it is used exactly (implicitly).

Stability function for the test equation:
\(y_{k+1} = y_k + \frac{z}{2}(y_k + y_{k+1}) \Rightarrow R(z) = \frac{1 + z/2}{1 - z/2}\)

For \(\text{Re}\,z < 0\) the numerator is smaller in magnitude than the denominator, so \(|R(z)| < 1\). The stability region is exactly the left half-plane – A-stable.
steps.insight: Implicit trapezoidal rule: order 2, \(R(z) = \frac{1 + z/2}{1 - z/2}\), A-stable.

steps.text: A catch of the trapezoidal rule shows up for very stiff components. As \(z \to -\infty\):
steps.formula: R(z) = \frac{1 + z/2}{1 - z/2} \;\longrightarrow\; -1 \qquad \text{(trapezoidal rule)}, \qquad R(z) = \frac{1}{1 - z} \;\longrightarrow\; 0 \qquad \text{(implicit Euler)}
steps.explanation:
Example \(\lambda = -50\), \(h = 0.05\) (\(z = -2.5\)): trapezoidal rule \(R = \frac{1 - 1.25}{1 + 1.25} \approx -0.11\), implicit Euler \(0.29\).

For \(\lambda = -1000\), \(h = 0.1\) (\(z = -100\)): trapezoidal rule \(R = \frac{-49}{51} \approx -0.96\). The fast component should vanish at once, but it is damped by only 4 % per step and jumps back and forth. Implicit Euler: \(R = \frac{1}{101} \approx 0.01\) – gone at once ✓

Methods with \(R(z) \to 0\) as \(z \to -\infty\) are called L-stable. For very stiff problems they are the better choice.
steps.insight: L-stable (\(R \to 0\) as \(z \to -\infty\)): very fast components are damped at once. Implicit Euler yes, trapezoidal rule no.

steps.text: Now we can pin down stiffness more precisely. Consider the system
steps.explanation:
The solution: \(y_1 = e^{-t}\) (slow), \(y_2 = e^{-1000t}\) (extremely fast). After \(t = 0.01\), \(y_2\) is practically zero, and from then on only \(y_1\) determines the behaviour.

For an accuracy of about \(10^{-3}\) on \([0, 10]\) a step size of about \(0.1\) would suffice for \(y_1\) (after a short initial phase with small steps).

But:
• Explicit: stability requires \(h \le \frac{2}{1000} = 0.002\) – for the whole 10 time units. That is \(5000\) steps.
• Implicit (A-stable): stability plays no role, \(h = 0.1\) suffices – \(100\) steps.

Even with the more expensive implicit steps one gains considerably.
steps.insight: Stiff: eigenvalues of very different size. Explicit methods must follow the fastest one, implicit ones only accuracy.

steps.text: A practical description of stiffness:
steps.explanation:
A system \(y' = f(t, y)\) is called stiff if
• all eigenvalues of the Jacobian have negative real part (the solution is stable),
• but some eigenvalues are much larger in magnitude than others,
• and the solution is to be followed over a long time compared with the fast time scales.

One measure is the stiffness ratio \(\frac{\max |\text{Re}\,\lambda|}{\min |\text{Re}\,\lambda|}\). In the example: \(\frac{1000}{1} = 1000\). In chemistry or circuit simulation ratios of \(10^{6}\) to \(10^{12}\) are common.

Rule of thumb in practice: if an explicit solver with step-size control takes extremely small steps although the solution looks smooth, the problem is probably stiff. Then switch to an implicit solver (e.g. ode15s instead of ode45 in MATLAB).
steps.insight: Telltale sign: an explicit solver becomes extremely slow although the solution is smooth.

steps.text: Quick check: is the system \(y' = Ay\) with \(A = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & 1 \\ 0 & -2000 \end{pmatrix}\) stiff? What step size does explicit Euler need?
steps.explanation:
\(A\) is upper triangular, so the eigenvalues are on the diagonal: \(-2\) and \(-2000\).

• Both negative: the solution decays ✓
• Stiffness ratio: \(\frac{2000}{2} = 1000\) – stiff.
• Explicit Euler needs \(h \le \frac{2}{2000} = 0.001\), although the slow component \(e^{-2t}\) would be resolved well with \(h \approx 0.05\).
steps.insight: Stiffness is recognised from the eigenvalues: all real parts negative, but of very different size.

steps.text: Finally, a different family of methods. One-step methods throw away all information after each step and start anew. Multistep methods instead use the earlier values already computed.
steps.explanation:
The idea: the slopes \(f_k = f(t_k, y_k)\), \(f_{k-1}\), … of the last steps are already known. One puts an interpolating polynomial through them (lesson “Polynomial Interpolation”) and integrates it over the next step.

Advantage: only one new function evaluation per step – even at higher order. RK4 needs four.
steps.insight: Multistep methods: reuse earlier slopes – one evaluation per step.

steps.text: The simplest example is the Adams–Bashforth method of order 2 (AB2):
steps.explanation:
Derivation: the line through the points \((t_{k-1}, f_{k-1})\) and \((t_k, f_k)\) is integrated over \([t_k, t_{k+1}]\). This gives \(h \cdot \left(f_k + \frac{f_k - f_{k-1}}{2}\right) = \frac{h}{2}(3f_k - f_{k-1})\) – an extrapolation of the slope.

One problem: the first step needs two starting values \(y_0\) and \(y_1\). The second is computed with a one-step method (e.g. RK4).

Example \(y' = y\), \(h = 0.1\), start \(y_0 = 1\), \(y_1 = e^{0.1} = 1.105171\):
\(y_2 = 1.105171 + 0.05 \cdot (3 \cdot 1.105171 - 1) \approx 1.220947\) (exact \(1.221403\))

Up to \(t = 1\): \(y_{10} \approx 2.70881\), error \(-0.0095\) – order 2 with only one evaluation per step.
steps.insight: AB2: \(y_{k+1} = y_k + \frac{h}{2}(3f_k - f_{k-1})\). Needs an additional starting value.

steps.text: Further multistep methods:
steps.explanation:
• Adams–Bashforth (explicit): orders 1 to about 5. AB1 is the explicit Euler method. Like all explicit methods, with a small stability region.

• Adams–Moulton (implicit): the interpolating polynomial also contains the new point \(f_{k+1}\). More accurate and more stable. The implicit trapezoidal rule is Adams–Moulton of order 2.

• Predictor–corrector: estimate \(y_{k+1}\) with Adams–Bashforth (predictor) and plug the value into Adams–Moulton (corrector) instead of solving the implicit equation exactly. This is cheap, but no longer A-stable.

• BDF methods (backward differentiation formulas): implicit, specifically for stiff problems. Instead of interpolating \(f\), one interpolates \(y\) and requires the derivative at the new point to satisfy the ODE.
steps.insight: Adams–Bashforth (explicit), Adams–Moulton (implicit), BDF (implicit, for stiff problems).

steps.text: The BDF method of order 2 (BDF2) is one of the workhorses for stiff problems:
steps.explanation:
On the left is an approximation of the derivative \(y'(t_{k+1})\) from three points (the derivative of the interpolating parabola). On the right the ODE at the new point.

BDF2 is A-stable and strongly damps very fast components (L-stable). BDF1 is exactly the implicit Euler method.

Example \(y' = -50y\), \(h = 0.05\), with \(y_0 = 1\) and \(y_1 = 0.2857\) (from implicit Euler): solving for \(y_{k+1}\) gives \(y_{k+1} = \frac{4y_k - y_{k-1}}{3 + 2h \cdot 50} = \frac{4y_k - y_{k-1}}{8}\).
\(y_2 = \frac{4 \cdot 0.2857 - 1}{8} \approx 0.018\) – stable and decaying fast.

Modern solvers for stiff problems (e.g. ode15s in MATLAB) use BDF methods of orders 1 to 5 with variable order and step size.
steps.insight: BDF2: \(\frac{3y_{k+1} - 4y_k + y_{k-1}}{2h} = f_{k+1}\) – A-stable, order 2, standard for stiff problems.

steps.text: Can A-stability and high order be combined arbitrarily in multistep methods? Unfortunately not.
steps.explanation:
Dahlquist's second barrier (1963): a linear multistep method that is A-stable has order at most 2. Among all A-stable methods of order 2, the trapezoidal rule has the smallest error constant.

That is why BDF3 to BDF5 are no longer fully A-stable – but their stability region contains almost the whole left half-plane, which is enough for most stiff problems.

Whoever needs A-stability with high order uses implicit Runge–Kutta methods (e.g. Radau methods). They are more expensive per step but are not subject to the Dahlquist barrier.

In addition, every multistep method must be zero-stable, otherwise “parasitic” solutions grow even as \(h \to 0\). For Adams and BDF methods (up to order 6) this holds.
steps.insight: Dahlquist barrier: A-stable linear multistep methods have order at most 2.

steps.text: Look back at what you can do now:
steps.explanation:
1. Test equation \(y' = \lambda y\) and stability function \(R(z)\), \(z = h\lambda\). Stable if \(|R(z)| \le 1\).

2. Explicit Euler: \(R = 1 + z\), stability region a disc around \(-1\); for real \(\lambda < 0\): \(h \le \frac{2}{|\lambda|}\). All explicit methods have bounded stability regions.

3. Imaginary eigenvalues (oscillations) lie outside the Euler region – hence the energy growth.

4. Implicit Euler: \(R = \frac{1}{1 - z}\), A-stable and L-stable. Trapezoidal rule: \(R = \frac{1 + z/2}{1 - z/2}\), A-stable, order 2. One (non)linear system per step.

5. Stiffness: eigenvalues with negative real part and very different size. Then use implicit methods.

6. Multistep methods: Adams–Bashforth, Adams–Moulton, BDF. Dahlquist barrier: A-stable ⇒ order \(\le 2\).
steps.insight: Key message: not stiff ⇒ explicit Runge–Kutta (ode45). Stiff ⇒ implicit, e.g. BDF (ode15s).

steps.text: With this you have completed the Numerical Analysis course. A brief look at the common thread:
steps.explanation:
• Error analysis: rounding, conditioning, stability – they decide whether a result can be trusted.
• Linear algebra: Gauss and LU, norms and condition numbers, QR, iterative solvers, eigenvalues.
• Nonlinear equations: bisection, fixed points, Newton – in one and in several dimensions.
• Approximating functions: interpolation, splines, quadrature.
• Differential equations: Runge–Kutta, stability, implicit and multistep methods.

The same ideas came up again and again: linearise (Newton, implicit methods), interpolate (quadrature, multistep methods), iterate until convergence, order and extrapolation, and the question whether a problem is well-conditioned and a method stable.
steps.insight: Numerical analysis means: computing – and always knowing how accurate the result is.
